questions.stem: Installing apps from unofficial stores or websites instead of the official app store is called what, and why is it risky?

choices.text: Sideloading; you have no assurance of what's really inside the package
Rooting; it speeds up the phone

questions.explanation: Sideloading is installing apps from unofficial sources - like buying medicine from a street vendor, you have no idea what's really inside.
questions.trap: Rooting is disabling the device's built-in security; sideloading is specifically installing from unofficial sources.

questions.stem: Intentionally disabling a phone's built-in security is called 'rooting' on Android. What is the equivalent term on iOS?
questions.explanation: On Android it's called rooting; on iOS it's jailbreaking. Both give full control over the OS but shatter its built-in defenses.
questions.trap: Sideloading is installing unofficial apps; the act of removing the OS's security restrictions on iOS is jailbreaking.

questions.stem: A malicious app is disguised to look like a legitimate one. What is this technique called?
questions.explanation: Application spoofing is when malicious apps are disguised as legitimate ones to trick users into installing them.
questions.trap: Jailbreaking disables OS security; disguising a malicious app as a legit one is application spoofing.

questions.stem: A user gets a data-usage-limit notification and notices high network traffic even though their habits haven't changed. What might this indicate?

choices.text: Malware may be sending personal files to an attacker

questions.explanation: A sudden spike in network traffic or an unexpected data-limit notification is a classic compromise symptom - malware could be exfiltrating personal files.
questions.trap: Unexpected high data usage is a red flag for malware, not a battery-saving behavior.

questions.stem: A phone is sluggish and a restart doesn't help. Combined with other symptoms, what could this indicate?

choices.text: Malware consuming CPU and memory in the background

questions.explanation: Degraded performance that a restart doesn't fix can mean malware is consuming CPU and memory in the background.
questions.trap: The number of saved contacts and the wallpaper have no bearing on background CPU/memory consumption.

questions.stem: Why might a malware-infected phone show limited or no internet connectivity?

choices.text: The malware is conserving the battery
The malware blocks access to prevent you from downloading security updates
The phone automatically enabled airplane mode for safety
The screen protector is interfering with the antenna

questions.explanation: Some malware blocks internet access specifically to prevent you from downloading security updates or removal tools.
questions.trap: It's a deliberate defensive move by the malware, not a battery-saving or hardware issue.

questions.stem: A sudden flood of pop-up ads everywhere on the phone is a dead giveaway for what?
questions.explanation: A sudden high number of ads popping up everywhere is a dead giveaway for adware.
questions.trap: A failing battery or cracked screen are hardware issues; a flood of ads points to adware.

questions.stem: A user suspects a deep infection or that their data has been leaked. What is the only way to be 100% sure the threat is gone?
questions.explanation: For symptoms of a deeper infection or a suspected data leak, the only way to be 100% sure is a factory reset, which wipes everything and restores the original clean state.
questions.trap: For minor adware, removing the offending app may suffice, but a deep infection requires a full factory reset.

questions.stem: After a factory reset following a data leak, what two actions must the user take immediately?

choices.text: Reinstall the same sideloaded apps and disable updates
Change passwords for all synced cloud accounts and enable MFA everywhere possible
Jailbreak the device and remove antivirus
Turn off the screen lock to save time

questions.explanation: After a reset and especially after a data leak, immediately change the passwords for all synced cloud accounts and enable MFA everywhere you can.
questions.trap: Reinstalling sideloaded apps or jailbreaking would reintroduce the very risks that caused the problem.

questions.stem: What is the best prevention practice to avoid mobile malware in the first place?

choices.text: Only use official app stores and never jailbreak or root the device
Sideload apps from many sources for variety
Share one password across all accounts

questions.explanation: Protect the phone by only using official app stores and never jailbreaking or rooting it.
questions.trap: Sideloading widely and disabling updates are exactly the behaviors that invite malware.
